channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Fireworks are an underestimated danger to public health, warn experts
item.description: Fireworks pose an underestimated danger to public health and require stronger regulations and sustained public education campaigns to help prevent devastating yet entirely avoidable injuries, warn U.S. experts in The BMJ.

item.title: Replacing dairy products with unfortified plant-based alternatives could lead to deficiencies in certain nutrients
item.description: Replacing dairy products, even partially, with unfortified plant-based alternatives may lead to a deficiency in vital nutrients, a new study from the University of Surrey reports. Mandatory fortification of plant-based alternatives and other foods, including bread, could lessen the risk of deficiencies, particularly iodine deficiency.

item.title: Shockwave therapy may ease frozen shoulder pain, but lasting benefits remain uncertain
item.description: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy probably reduces short-term pain linked to frozen shoulder, while manipulation under anesthesia—with or without steroid injections—probably improves short-term flexion (raising the arm forward and overhead) compared with usual care, finds a review of the latest trial evidence published by The BMJ.

item.title: How a CRISPR sickle cell therapy moved from lab to clinical trial
item.description: A UCLA-led team has described how it advanced an experimental CRISPR approach for sickle cell disease into a blood stem cell therapy that can be manufactured at the scale and quality required for a clinical trial.

item.title: Why humans are more sensitive than other species to a brain developmental disease
item.description: Researchers at VIB and KU Leuven have uncovered how mutations in the ASPM gene disrupt the development of neural stem cells that help the human brain grow. This disruption explains how these mutations cause microcephaly, a condition characterized by an abnormally small brain and head, often accompanied by intellectual disability. The discovery, published in Developmental Cell, also sheds light on how differences in brain development can make humans more susceptible to certain genetic conditions than other mammals.

item.title: From DNA marks to RNA control: A new clue to acute myeloid leukemia
item.description: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is an aggressive blood cancer in which abnormal, immature cells build up in the bone marrow, disrupting the production of healthy blood cells. Now, a new study, led by Dr. José Luis Sardina's group at the Josep Carreras Leukaemia Research Institute (IJC), examines how two systems that help control normal blood cell development are connected: the chemical marks on DNA and the regulation of RNA, which carries instructions for making proteins. The work is published in the journal Science Advances.

item.title: Combining HIV prevention and addiction treatment in mobile clinics could save lives
item.description: Results from a clinical trial in five major United States cities show that delivering integrated HIV and substance use disorder (SUD) services using peer navigation in mobile medical units reduced all-cause deaths by 71% compared with those among participants who received peer navigation to community-based services alone. While scientists found no difference in the use of daily, oral preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD) between the groups, the secondary outcome of reduced mortality was significant. The study is published in JAMA Psychiatry.

item.title: Tiny structures in our spines could hold clues to why our backs wear out
item.description: An international team of scientists has discovered how some of the tiniest structures in the human spine help it cope with the strain of bending, lifting and everyday movement, potentially shedding new light on why spinal disks deteriorate.

item.title: Chronic illness linked to higher prescription drug misuse
item.description: Working-age adults who manage more chronic health conditions are more likely to misuse prescription medications, researchers in the Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs found.

item.title: Protein DUSP4 boosts cancer-fighting T cells in colorectal cancer lab models
item.description: The immune system has powerful cells that can recognize and destroy cancer, but this ability can gradually wane when the cells reside within a tumor. Researchers from the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (NUS Medicine), and their collaborators have identified a protein that could help keep these cancer-fighting immune cells active and potentially provide a new way to strengthen engineered T-cell therapies against colorectal cancer.

item.title: Generative AI fills gaps in brain wiring maps where MRI scans lose signal
item.description: Researchers from the Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute (Stevens INI) at the Keck School of Medicine of USC have developed an artificial intelligence (AI) model that helps fill gaps in brain wiring maps made with diffusion MRI, a type of scan that traces the brain's nerve fiber pathways. This could help researchers study how key brain connections change with aging and disease.

item.title: WHO hails progress against neglected tropical diseases
item.description: The World Health Organization on Wednesday celebrated "major progress" against neglected tropical diseases, with some like sleeping sickness all but disappearing, but urged more investment and faster and broader action.

item.title: Exposure to petroleum-based lubricants at work associated with multiple sclerosis risk
item.description: Exposure to petroleum-derived lubricants at work, including engine oil, hydraulic oil and cutting fluids used to cool or lubricate metal during metalworking, is associated with higher odds of multiple sclerosis (MS), according to a study published in Neurology. The study does not prove that exposure to these lubricants causes MS. It only shows an association.

item.title: WHO approves clinical trials on two new Ebola vaccines
item.description: The World Health Organization on Wednesday approved clinical trials for two new Ebola vaccines, as doctors fight to control an outbreak in Africa that has killed more than 5,300 people.

item.title: Longer estrogen exposure linked to better brain vessel health in older women
item.description: Women who had a longer reproductive period and had used or are using hormone replacement therapy showed fewer signs of damage to the small blood vessels in the brain later in life. This is shown by a study led by researchers at Karolinska Institutet, published in the journal Neurology.

item.title: Some 1,800 dead from cholera in Ebola-hit DR Congo: WHO
item.description: Cholera has killed around 1,800 people so far this year in the Democratic Republic of Congo, which is also battling its deadliest Ebola outbreak, the World Health Organization said Wednesday.

item.title: Blood pressure medication and vibration may boost brain waste clearance
item.description: The brain's own clearance mechanisms are most active during sleep. Researchers have now shown that this natural clearance process can also be enhanced while people are awake. A novel vasomechanical treatment increased the removal of harmful proteins from participants' brains.

item.title: Frankfurt says airport malaria cases likely from West Africa
item.description: Eight malaria cases around Frankfurt airport this summer—three of them fatal—were likely caused by parasites originating in West Africa, the city authorities said Wednesday.

item.title: WHO sounds alarm over lack of physical activity among teens
item.description: A quarter of teens globally engage in basically no physical activity—not even an hour of exercise a week—the World Health Organization said Wednesday, warning that this significantly raises health risks.

item.title: AI starts writing acne prescriptions without a doctor's visit in one state
item.description: Utah has become the first state to let an artificial intelligence (AI) program prescribe medication without a doctor writing the prescription, starting with acne treatments.

item.title: New CRISPR proteins expand editing access to heart disease genes
item.description: Rice University's Han Xiao has used his AI-supported Sequence Display technology to expand the targeting abilities of CRISPR/Cas9. In a paper recently published in Nature Communications, Xiao evolved several variants of a compact Cas9 that could efficiently target stretches of DNA previously inaccessible for editing. The research included a proof-of-concept study in which the evolved Cas9s were successfully used to edit two genes found in coronary heart disease.

item.title: Key gene preserves lifelong supply of stem cells that make bone healing possible, study suggests
item.description: The action of a key gene is required to maintain a lifelong supply of stem cells that make bone healing possible, a new study finds.

item.title: Rapid tau spread may explain why midlife Alzheimer's progresses more rapidly
item.description: Patients with early-onset Alzheimer's disease, whose symptoms start before age 65, have more extensive deposits of tau, a hallmark protein of the condition, compared with patients whose symptoms start at 65-plus, a new study found. What's more, tau accumulates at more than twice the rate in younger compared to older patients and spreads widely throughout the brain.

item.title: Experimental ultrasound implant could help guide care after spinal cord injury
item.description: A team of engineers and surgeons from Johns Hopkins Medicine has published its first proof-of-concept study that shows temporarily implanting a tiny ultrasonic device into the location of a spinal cord injury can be feasible, safe and potentially useful. These findings, which mark an early midpoint in a multitiered research journey to develop and study how the device could be used in clinical care, were published in Science Advances.

item.title: From green smoothies to stem‑cell supplements—online 'immune‑boosting' ideas may lead you astray
item.description: We all want a well-functioning immune system to help us fight invasive bacteria and viruses and recover faster from illness. Popular "immune-boosting" ideas, however, might be more of a hindrance than a help.

item.title: Proning and high-frequency oscillation may not reduce duration of ventilation for children with lung injury
item.description: A treatment that is part of standard care for adults with acute respiratory distress syndrome does not provide the same benefit in children. Children with severe acute lung injury placed in the prone position do not spend less time dependent on a ventilator. High-frequency oscillatory ventilation does not shorten the duration of mechanical ventilation either. This is shown by a worldwide study led, among others, by UMCG pediatric intensivist Dr. Martin Kneyber. The results were published in The Lancet.

item.title: What science says about perimenopause, menopause and mood swings—minus the hype
item.description: After decades of relative neglect, menopause is suddenly everywhere—in the news, on social media and in conversations among friends. Some are calling it the "meno-boom," and booms attract business.

item.title: AI improves questionnaire-based Parkinson's screening while working around missing answers
item.description: Scientists at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI) have developed an artificial intelligence model to streamline and improve screening for Parkinson's disease (PD) so doctors can refer patients for early-stage testing.

item.title: New drug-development strategy might protect neurons by displacing proteins that inhibit helpful enzymes
item.description: Researchers from the University of California, Berkeley may have discovered a new strategy for treating complex neurodegenerative diseases. Their study, recently published in Science, describes a new approach that allows specialized enzymes to clear out several disease-causing proteins. So far, the method has proved useful for protecting neurons in lab tests.

item.title: How your brain learned to love coffee, chocolate, fat and sugar
item.description: If you can remember your first sip of coffee, the memory might not be a pleasant one. Coffee's bitter flavor is one we naturally steer clear of. So how do coffee fans learn to love it? The answer may lie in an understudied "slow" dopamine pathway connecting the gut and brain. A new study from UC San Francisco shows that this pathway helps the brain connect a flavor with the beneficial effects that follow ingesting it.
